title: Out of Bell Labs
question: How did five ideas from one New Jersey lab end up running the world?

intro.label: Why this one
intro.author: Matthew Kenney
intro.status: DRAFT, run through writing-check before it ships
paragraphs: I live about five miles from Thomas Edison's laboratory in West Orange. He opened it in 1887 as an invention factory, with a library, machine shops and a factory next door, and more than half of his 1,093 patents came out of it. By World War One the complex employed 10,000 people.

Thirty-eight years after Edison opened West Orange, AT&T built the same idea at a scale he never imagined, and in 1941 it moved it to Murray Hill. I have spent eleven and a half years in corporate innovation, which mostly means watching big companies try to rebuild what Bell Labs had.
California runs the table now. But for a small, crowded state, New Jersey punches way above its weight. This page follows five ideas out of one New Jersey lab and asks how each one left the building.

stations.title: A lab with no stock ticker
stations.who: Frank Jewett, first president. Owned half by AT&T, half by Western Electric.
stations.what: On January 1, 1925, AT&T folds the engineering departments of AT&T and Western Electric into one company, Bell Telephone Laboratories. You could not buy its stock.
stations.pitch: Bell Labs would develop equipment for Western Electric and plan the network for AT&T, and those two companies would pay its bills.
stations.spread: Its starting budget was about $12 million, which Jon Gertner puts at roughly $150 million in today's money. From the start it was several labs in different places, not one building.

stations.title: The man who built the place
stations.where: Director of research, Bell Telephone Laboratories
stations.what: A vacuum tube physicist from Princeton, Missouri is named director of research in 1936. He starts hiring young PhDs in a field Bell barely had, solid state physics. His first hire is William Shockley.
stations.pitch: Hire a critical mass of brilliant people, put the thinkers and the builders under one roof, and point them at what is not yet known. Kelly called it an institute of creative technology.
stations.spread: After the war he reorganized the labs around a new solid state group. He became president in 1951 and chairman in 1959. On his watch Bell produced the transistor, the solar cell and the laser.

stations.title: Murray Hill
stations.what: The New Jersey campus opens in 1941.
stations.pitch: Research and development, side by side, on one campus.
stations.spread: It stays the home of Bell Labs for more than 80 years and hosts the transistor and the laser.

stations.title: The government opens the vault
stations.what: Settling a seven-year antitrust case, AT&T must license all its existing patents royalty free and stay out of every business except telecommunications.
stations.pitch: Free the monopoly's inventions without breaking up the monopoly.
stations.spread: 7,820 patents, about 1.3 percent of all unexpired US patents, became free to use. Follow-on innovation building on them rose 17 percent, driven mainly by young and small companies, and almost entirely outside telecom equipment.

stations.title: Ma Bell comes apart
stations.what: The Bell System breaks up. Bell Labs becomes part of AT&T Technologies, and the Bell cellular licenses pass to the new regional phone companies.
stations.pitch: Split the phone monopoly into pieces.
stations.spread: In 1996 most of Bell Labs went to Lucent Technologies. Lucent merged with Alcatel in 2006, and Nokia bought Alcatel-Lucent in 2016.

stations.title: Back to the city
stations.where: HELIX, New Brunswick, New Jersey, next to Rutgers
stations.what: Ground was broken September 4, 2025 on a 10 story, 370,000 square foot headquarters. The move out of Murray Hill is planned for 2028.
stations.pitch: Researchers do better work close to universities, startups and partners than on a suburban campus.
stations.spread: Nokia says the work there will include quantum, photonics, optics, 6G and AI. It stays in New Jersey after Nokia looked at 25 locations.

stations.title: The transistor
stations.who: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, with their supervisor William Shockley
stations.what: A half inch device of germanium and gold that amplified a signal about 100 times. They showed it to Bell executives on December 23, 1947.
stations.pitch: A solid state replacement for the vacuum tube.
stations.spread: Bell announced it on June 30, 1948. Shockley followed with the junction transistor, easier to manufacture, announced in 1951. The three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

stations.title: The transistor goes on sale
stations.what: Commercial production of junction transistors for portable radios.
stations.pitch: Electronics you can carry.
stations.spread: Under seven years from a lab bench in New Jersey to a product sold by a company in Texas.

stations.title: West to Mountain View
stations.where: Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory, Mountain View, California
stations.what: Backed by Beckman Instruments, Shockley, who had left Bell Labs, opens Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory in Mountain View, near Stanford. It is the same year the consent decree frees the transistor patents.
stations.pitch: Silicon devices, made by a startup.
stations.spread: The Benton Institute argues that the decree's royalty-free transistor licenses are a missing piece of how Silicon Valley got its start.

stations.title: The most made thing in history
stations.where: Estimate by analyst Jim Handy, via the Computer History Museum
stations.what: About 13 sextillion transistors shipped, more than 99.9 percent of them MOS devices.
stations.pitch: Billions of switches on every chip in every phone and AI server.
stations.spread: A sextillion is a one followed by 21 zeros. The 2014 estimate was 2.9 sextillion, and the total grows by billions every day.

stations.title: The bit
stations.where: Bell System Technical Journal, July and October 1948
stations.what: “A Mathematical Theory of Communication,” which defined information entropy and redundancy and put the word bit into print.
stations.pitch: Communication is a statistical process you can measure, whatever the message means.
stations.spread: Shannon had mostly finished the paper at Bell Labs by the end of 1944. He credited the word bit to his colleague John Tukey.

stations.title: From A theory to The theory
stations.what: The paper becomes a book, retitled The Mathematical Theory of Communication once its generality was clear, with an essay by Warren Weaver for general readers.
stations.pitch: A theory for every kind of signal, not just the phone network.
stations.spread: The paper is treated as the founding work of information theory as a field.

stations.title: The solar cell
stations.who: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson
stations.where: Bell Labs in Berkeley Heights, announced at Murray Hill
stations.what: The first practical silicon solar cell, about 6 percent efficient. On April 25, 1954 it powered a toy Ferris wheel and a radio transmitter.
stations.pitch: Power for phone equipment in remote, humid places, where dry cell batteries kept failing.
stations.spread: Fuller and Pearson were doping silicon for transistors. Pearson saw the effect and told Chapin to stop wasting time on selenium.

stations.title: Saved by the space race
stations.who: U.S. Navy Vanguard program. Hoffman Electronics held the license to sell the cells.
stations.what: A 3.5 pound satellite carrying six solar cells.
stations.pitch: A satellite that keeps talking after its battery dies.
stations.spread: Its battery-powered radio fell silent within months. The solar-powered one kept transmitting until 1964. Before that, high cost had kept the cells to toys and demos.

stations.title: Two inventions fly together
stations.what: The first active, direct relay communications satellite, powered by 3,600 solar cells and carrying 1,000 transistors.
stations.pitch: Bounce a microwave signal, and television, across the ocean.
stations.spread: Bell scientist John Pierce's idea went from theory to working satellite in two years.

stations.title: Terawatts
stations.where: IEEE Electron Devices Society, 70th anniversary note
stations.what: Worldwide silicon solar installations have passed the terawatt mark.
stations.pitch: Electricity from sunlight, cheap enough for rooftops.
stations.spread: Cell efficiency has risen about 0.3 percent a year since 1954.

stations.title: Unix on a spare PDP-7
stations.who: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, with Doug McIlroy and Joe Ossanna
stations.where: Bell Labs, after it pulled out of the Multics project
stations.what: A small new operating system, soon called Unix, begun in the summer of 1969.
stations.pitch: Something smaller and simpler than Multics, built for their own use.
stations.spread: Thompson started by writing a game, Space Travel, for the machine.

stations.title: Portable software
stations.where: Bell Labs. Shown outside at a symposium in October 1973.
stations.what: Unix is rewritten in C, the language Ritchie built for it, so it can move from one kind of computer to another.
stations.pitch: Write the system once, run it on many machines.
stations.spread: Barred from the computer business by its antitrust agreement, AT&T could not sell Unix as a product. Version 6 in 1975 was the first to spread widely outside Bell Labs.

stations.title: Berkeley takes it over
stations.what: The Berkeley line of Unix begins. AT&T later licenses Unix to Microsoft, Sun, HP and IBM too.
stations.pitch: A Unix that universities could improve and pass around.
stations.spread: Ken Thompson spent a sabbatical year teaching operating systems at Berkeley in 1975 and 1976.

stations.title: Inside the Mac and the phone
stations.where: Darwin, the core of Mac OS X
stations.what: Apple releases Darwin, a Unix system that becomes the core of Mac OS X, now macOS.
stations.pitch: A solid, proven core under a friendly interface.
stations.spread: The Computer History Museum counts Linux, Android, BSD, macOS and iOS among Unix's descendants. Linux copies the design but carries no Bell Labs or Berkeley code.

stations.title: Hexagons
stations.who: W. Rae Young and Douglas H. Ring
stations.what: A grid of hexagonal cells, each with a low power transmitter, handing a call from one cell to the next as a car drives through.
stations.pitch: Reuse the same radio frequencies over and over across a city, so many more people can have a mobile phone.
stations.spread: The technology to build it did not exist yet, and the frequencies had not been allocated. It waited decades.

stations.title: Motorola calls Bell
stations.what: The first public call on a handheld cell phone, placed to Joel Engel, who ran AT&T's rival project.
stations.pitch: A phone that belongs to a person, not a car.
stations.spread: At Bell, Engel and Richard Frenkiel had rediscovered Ring's idea and developed it into a network of hexagonal cells.

stations.title: Cellular goes live
stations.what: The first modern commercial cellular system in the US opens in Chicago.
stations.pitch: Phone service that follows you.
stations.spread: Three months later the Bell System broke up, and its cellular licenses passed to the new regional phone companies.

stations.title: 9.2 billion
stations.where: International Telecommunication Union, Facts and Figures 2025
stations.what: 9.2 billion mobile cellular subscriptions, 112 for every 100 people on Earth.
stations.pitch: A phone in every pocket.
stations.spread: Mobile broadband is 89 percent of them, and 36 percent of mobile broadband is now 5G.

series.label: US real GDP
series.note: Annual, from the Bureau of Economic Analysis via FRED. The series starts in 1929, four years after Bell Labs. It shows the economy the inventions grew into, not how much of it they caused.

counterpoints.claim: The monopoly paid for the miracles. AT&T's huge resources as the phone monopoly let Bell Labs do basic research with only loose ties to phone service. When the company shrank, so did the pure research.
The same monopoly sat on its own market. After 1956 innovation rose outside telecom, but not in telecom equipment, where Bell kept shutting competitors out.

Inventing is not scaling. Texas Instruments sold the first transistor radios, Hoffman sold the solar cells, Motorola made the first handheld cell call and Apple put Unix in the Mac. Bell often invented the thing other people turned into products.
Bell was not the only place the transistor could have come from. A point-contact transistor was invented independently in 1948.

open_questions: Verify the $12 million 1925 budget directly in The Idea Factory. Right now it comes from a reposted excerpt (source 3).
Find a sourced modern landing for information theory, such as how Shannon's limits shape the coding in 5G or Wi-Fi. The thread stops in 1949.
Laser and CCD are the obvious alternates for the top five. Source who built the first working laser before adding it.
Name the 1948 independent inventors of the transistor from a primary source.
One source credits Eero Saarinen with Murray Hill. Saarinen designed Holmdel. Do not use until verified.
HELIX timing conflicts: NJBIZ says construction completes in 2027, Nokia says the move happens by 2028.
NEEDS SOURCE for the New Jersey claim: patents or R&D spending per capita by state, New Jersey against California and Massachusetts.
